identity.name: Transparency Coalition (TCAI) — Do Not Train Standard
identity.originator: Transparency Coalition for AI (TCAI). Coalition includes publishers, content creators, and advocacy organisations.
identity.year: 2024 (DNT standard advocacy); 2024 (Virginia HB 2250); 2024 (California AB 2013 training data transparency).
identity.key_text: TCAI position papers on Do Not Train data and Training Data Request prompts. Virginia Consumer Opt-Out Artificial Intelligence Training Data Act (HB 2250). California AB 2013.

conceptual.core_claim: Content owners should have a machine-readable, universal mechanism to declare their work off-limits for AI training — analogous to robots.txt for web crawling or copyright pages in publishing — enforceable through both industry standards and legislation.
conceptual.relation_to_attention_economy: TCAI operates within and responds to the attention economy's latest phase: the extraction of creative content for AI training. The DNT standard is a defensive mechanism against a new form of attention-economy extraction — using creative outputs not to attract eyeballs but to train models that may replace the creators. It represents a consent-based limit on extractive infrastructure.
conceptual.relation_to_commons: Complicated. TCAI primarily represents content owners asserting property rights, which can conflict with commons principles. The DNT standard defaults to enclosure (opt-out of training = keeping content private), whereas a commons approach might default to sharing with conditions. However, TCAI also advocates for transparency (Training Data Verification Requests), which serves commons interests by making the AI training pipeline legible.
conceptual.epistemological_stance: Legal-regulatory. Knowledge is structured as rights, permissions, and compliance. Validity is determined by legal enforceability and industry adoption. The epistemological framework is copyright law extended to AI training contexts.

technical.architecture_pattern: Machine-readable metadata standard (analogous to robots.txt). Proposed mechanisms: Do Not Train (DNT) tags in content metadata; Training Data Verification Request (TDVR) protocols; Training Data Deletion Request (TDDR) protocols. Regulatory compliance layer, not a data system.
technical.data_model: Metadata annotations on existing content. Binary signals (train/do-not-train) attached to content at the file, page, or domain level. Verification and deletion request protocols add request-response patterns. The data model is simple and declarative — it does not describe the content, only its training-permission status.
technical.temporal_logic: Regulatory-reactive. Standards emerge in response to AI training practices that are already occurring. The temporal logic is backward-looking: DNT is applied after content has been created and after AI training has become a threat. There is an inherent temporal asymmetry — once a model is trained on content, it cannot 'unlearn' it, so DNT is only effective prospectively.
technical.absence_handling: DNT does not handle absence — it is a presence/absence signal (tag present = do not train; tag absent = ambiguous/implicit consent). The framework does not address what happens when training data lacks DNT tags — is silence consent? This ambiguity is a core vulnerability.
technical.scalability_model: Centralised standard with decentralised implementation. The standard is designed to be adopted industry-wide, but compliance depends on individual AI developers choosing to respect the tags. Enforcement is regulatory, not technical.

garden_logic_comparative.layer_mapping: participation. DNT maps to A(DAI)'s participation layer because it defines the terms under which content can enter the system. It is a consent mechanism that sits at the intake boundary, not a sensing or substrate component.
garden_logic_comparative.intention_vs_attention: TCAI operates within attention-economy logic — it is a defensive response to extractive AI training, not a positive alternative. The DNT standard does not generate intention; it prevents unwanted extraction. However, the transparency mechanisms (TDVR, TDDR) have intention-aligned potential: they make the AI training pipeline structurally legible, which serves diagnostic purposes. A(DAI) should view DNT as a necessary hygiene standard for its intake pipeline, not as a model for its core logic.
garden_logic_comparative.coherence_vs_consensus: Consensus-seeking. TCAI aims for industry-wide adoption of a single standard — this is a consensus project. The DNT tag is binary (yes/no), not gradated or interpretive. This is appropriate for a consent mechanism but misaligned with A(DAI)'s coherence principle, which accommodates multiple readings.
garden_logic_comparative.contestability: Low contestability in the standard itself — DNT is meant to be unambiguous. But highly contested in the regulatory environment — AI companies resist DNT mandates, and the legal status of training as 'fair use' remains unresolved. The framework's outputs are not contestable (a DNT tag means what it means), but its legitimacy is hotly contested.
garden_logic_comparative.forkability: Not forkable. The DNT standard is designed to be universal and uniform — forks would undermine its purpose. Different jurisdictions may implement different regulatory versions, but these are not 'forks' in the commons sense.
garden_logic_comparative.tendency_axis_position: openness: tends toward enclosure — DNT defaults to restricting access. However, the transparency mechanisms push toward openness by making AI training pipelines legible. commons: ambiguous — serves individual property rights more than collective commons governance. But protects the creative commons from extractive AI training. spectacle vs infrastructure: infrastructure — DNT is an invisible metadata standard. individual vs distributed: individual — DNT is exercised by individual content owners, not collectively.
garden_logic_comparative.what_adai_should_adopt: Respect for DNT tags in the intake pipeline — A(DAI) must not ingest content marked as Do Not Train. The principle of machine-readable consent as a first-class element of the data pipeline. The TDVR concept: any contributor to A(DAI)'s graph should be able to query whether their content has been ingested and how it has been processed. The general principle that consent is not just ethical but architecturally necessary — it must be mechanically enforced, not just promised in a policy document.
garden_logic_comparative.what_adai_should_refuse: The binary consent model. DNT is yes/no, but A(DAI) needs more nuanced consent: 'train but attribute', 'train for diagnosis but not for generation', 'share within this community but not beyond', 'use for 2 years then re-consent'. A(DAI) should build a richer consent vocabulary than DNT provides. Also refuse the property-rights framing — A(DAI) is a commons, not a marketplace. Consent in A(DAI) should be about collective governance, not individual intellectual property.
garden_logic_comparative.structural_tension: TCAI frames AI training as extraction to be restricted. A(DAI) frames knowledge contribution as a commons practice to be enabled. These are fundamentally different orientations: restriction vs. contribution. The tension is that A(DAI) must operate in a regulatory environment shaped by TCAI's extractive framing while building a commons alternative. A(DAI)'s intake pipeline must respect DNT (legal necessity) while also offering a positive alternative — a consent architecture that makes contribution attractive, not just extraction preventable.

critical.limits: DNT is easily ignored — compliance depends on goodwill or regulation, not technical enforcement. The tag provides no mechanism for verification or enforcement. Once a model is trained, content cannot be 'unlearned'. The binary model (train/do-not-train) does not capture the nuances of how content might be used. The standard addresses text and images but has unclear applicability to audio, video, and multi-modal content.
critical.who_is_excluded: Small creators and individual artists who lack the technical knowledge to implement DNT tags. Non-Western content creators who may not be aware of TCAI's standards or the legal frameworks they reference. Open-source and Creative Commons communities whose content is already freely available and may be caught in DNT overreach. Oral and performative cultures whose knowledge is not fixed in files that can carry metadata.
critical.failure_under_attention: [uncertain] If DNT becomes widely adopted, AI companies may route around it — training on content that lacks DNT tags (biasing toward content from those who do not know about DNT), using synthetic data, or negotiating bilateral licensing deals with major publishers while ignoring small creators. The standard could create a two-tier system: well-resourced publishers protect their content, while individual creators remain exposed. DNT becomes a corporate protection mechanism rather than a universal creative right.

governance.governance_model: Coalition-based advocacy pushing for regulatory mandates and industry standards. TCAI is a lobbying and standards organisation, not a governance body. Actual governance would come from legislation (Virginia, California) and industry compliance.
governance.consent_architecture: Machine-readable opt-out (Do Not Train tags). Request-response protocols for verification (TDVR) and deletion (TDDR). This is a consent architecture, but it is narrow — binary, retrospective, and individually exercised. No collective consent mechanism.

materiality.extraction_vector: Anti-extraction. TCAI exists to prevent the extraction of creative content for AI training. However, the coalition itself represents publishers and content owners, whose primary interest may be commercial licensing rather than creative rights per se. The extraction it prevents is AI training; the extraction it enables is traditional copyright licensing.
materiality.composability: Standard-level composability. DNT tags are simple metadata that can be added to any content format. The standard is designed to be universally adoptable. However, it does not compose with more nuanced consent systems — it is binary, not modular.
materiality.liveness: Active and growing. Legislative momentum in Virginia, California, and other states. TCAI continues to advocate for adoption. The DNT concept is gaining traction as AI training becomes more politically salient.
materiality.scale_of_operation: Field-level to planetary. TCAI aims for universal adoption across the AI training industry. Current adoption is concentrated in US publishing and media industries.
materiality.temporality: Regulatory-reactive and prospective. DNT is only effective for future training runs, not retroactively. The temporal logic is defensive: protecting content from future extraction rather than diagnosing past harms.
